# The Architect's Role {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones."*
>
> — Herbert A. Simon, *The Sciences of the Artificial*, 3rd ed. (1996) [@Simon1996SciencesArtificial, p. 111]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Herbert Simon defined design through the course from a
present situation to a preferred one. The definition places problem choice,
abstraction, boundaries, and product tradeoffs inside the technical work.
Automation can contribute substantially to that course. The architect's
technical contribution lies in shaping the course into a coherent system,
establishing what the evidence supports, and making the residual risk visible.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
If a capable AI-assisted design system can formulate studies, generate
artifacts, search design spaces, run tools, interpret failures, and recommend
a design, what technical work do architects still contribute?
:::

Grant the strongest premise in this book. A capable AI-assisted system can
perform substantial work from study formulation through technical
recommendation, including coordinating specialized methods, tools,
verification, and failure-driven revision across a long design study. Nothing
in this chapter depends on preserving a protected set of tasks that only people
can perform.

The architect's role is not whatever automation has failed to absorb. It is a
positive technical role. Architects frame the problem, choose the abstractions
and system boundaries, compose components and disciplines into one feasible
design, interpret disagreement and missing evidence, and state which
uncertainties remain. They shape both the system and the design process through
which it is developed.

Organizational assignments vary, and one person may hold more than one role.
That variability makes four distinct kinds of engineering work easy to
collapse. A *domain specialist* qualifies a result within a specific discipline
and owns any technical waiver or signoff there. *The architect* means the
qualified architect or architecture team that integrates those results across
the system. One lead architect may carry that view, or an architecture team may
divide it, but the scope of each judgment, required concurrence,
escalation path, and responsibility for end-to-end integration must
remain explicit.

The *commitment authority* is the named role or set of roles assigned to decide
whether a design advances. When architecture and product authority reside in
separate roles, the required product concurrence must remain explicit. The
*accountable organization* assigns and resources the specialist, architect,
and commitment roles, maintains their escalation paths, and remains answerable
for the consequences of the resulting product. Naming one person does not
transfer that organizational accountability.

The architect's distinctive output in this model is a supported architecture
recommendation. It names the design under consideration, the conditions and
evidence that support it, the remaining risk, and the evidence that must narrow
or reopen the recommendation. The named commitment authority then decides,
with the required product concurrence, whether the design advances.

Work moves among these four roles in both directions, but their technical
outputs and authority remain distinct. Domain specialists send qualified
results, failed checks, and unresolved assumptions toward system synthesis.
The architect sends reframed questions and requests for stronger checks back
to the specialists, retains direct access to the decisive artifacts and
failures, and integrates the cross-layer evidence into a supported technical
recommendation. The commitment authority receives that recommendation rather
than a decision made by implication. Monitoring and material changes can later
reopen the technical work, while the accountable organization keeps the roles,
resources, escalation paths, and product consequences connected
(@fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment).

![**Technical synthesis precedes commitment.** Domain specialists qualify
scoped results and checks. The architect frames the problem, chooses the
abstraction and system boundary, connects layers, interprets disagreement, and
states the residual risk before forming a supported technical recommendation.
A separate commitment authority advances, holds, or rejects the design. The
accountable organization resources these roles, and changed conditions can
reopen the technical work.](images/F11-architecture-synthesis-commitment.svg){#fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment width="100%" fig-alt="An accountable organization surrounds three distinct roles. Domain specialists qualify scoped results, checks, artifacts, and failures. An architect or architecture team frames the problem, chooses the abstraction and system boundary, connects layers, interprets disagreement, states residual risk, and retains access to decisive artifacts and failures. The supported technical recommendation then reaches a separate commitment authority that advances, holds, or rejects the design. Monitoring and changed conditions return to the architect and may reopen specialist work."}

The separation is not a one-way approval chain. A failed check can change the
problem or require another observation, and a later workload, software, tool,
process, implementation, or field change can invalidate the recommendation's
conditions. The commitment decision does not rewrite the qualified results that
supported it. The sections that follow develop the architect's central work,
and @tbl-architect-technical-judgments names the recurring judgments that turn
those results into a coherent product recommendation.

NASA systems-engineering guidance provides an established precedent for this
separation. Its decision-analysis process produces a comparison and may produce
a recommendation for a decision-making authority, while the decision authority
is the role authorized to make the consequential program or project decision
[@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, sec. 6.8 and app. B]. This precedent supports the
distinction between technical analysis and an authorized decision. It does not
prescribe an organization chart for a chip project.

Every component may work as intended and still fail to establish a coherent
product. A model can optimize a network link against the objective it was
given, a compiler can validate a lowering path, a verifier can return a
counterexample, and a physical-design flow can close timing. The architect
must determine whether these results describe one product under one consistent
set of workload, software, interface, memory, power, package, and product
assumptions.

Those locally qualified results cannot support a system recommendation on
their own. The architect must first frame the problem, choose the abstraction
and components, integrate across layers, and interpret disagreement. That
synthesis produces a technical recommendation while keeping specialist
results, the program claim, and the decision to advance distinct. Its scope and
support limit what the architect can recommend for commitment and identify
which later changes must reopen technical review.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Separate an architecture recommendation, specialist result or signoff,
  program claim, commitment decision, and organizational accountability.
- Frame an architecture problem whose workload, software path, system
  boundary, constraints, and decision remain coherent as AI and tools act.
- Choose abstractions, methods, components, interfaces, and checks that fit
  the technical problem rather than merely the available automation.
- Integrate specialist results across software, ISA, microarchitecture,
  memory, implementation, package, power, and product concerns.
- Interpret disagreement and uncertainty, state a bounded technical
  recommendation, and identify which later changes must reopen review.
:::

## Delegating Work Without Losing Technical Contact

Four conditions govern the assignment of design work. The architecture team
must be able to observe the candidate state, reverse a proposed change, reject
a bad result with independent checks, and bound the cross-layer consequences.
A bounded array-mapping sweep or tool run often meets these conditions and can
be performed by a method or domain specialist. Freezing a software-facing
interface is different. It is a difficult-to-reverse cross-layer decision that
hardens assumptions across compiler and runtime behavior, memory, RTL,
physical implementation, and product integration. A qualified architect or
architecture team must reconcile that evidence, and the commitment authority
must decide whether the transition proceeds. Both cases also depend on a team
competent to challenge assumptions and trace a failure beyond the delegated
boundary.

The assignment rule does not reserve a task for people or predict which jobs
automation can absorb. Instead, it keeps six architecture judgments connected
as work moves among people and tools. Architects formulate the system question,
choose representations and their acceptable omissions, select methods and
environments, require independent checks, integrate cross-layer results, and
decide what the combined work can support.

These judgments remain part of the engineering work because an architecture is
not the union of locally successful component outputs. It is a choice of
mechanisms and interfaces that work together under conditions the product will
encounter. Architects must inspect disagreement, exceptions, and model limits,
then determine which uncertainties the next design transition can carry.

The premise also changes how architects maintain technical contact with the
work. They need not perform every routine task manually, but they must remain
able to challenge a formulation, inspect decisive artifacts and failures,
trace a result across interfaces, and recognize when a model or check is being
used outside its support. Otherwise delegation removes the competence needed
to judge the design it produces.

Human-factors research distinguishes misuse, when people rely on automation
inappropriately, from disuse, when they neglect its capabilities
[@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation]. The distinction explains why
technical contact must survive delegation. It does not determine which
architecture decisions a person or an automated system should control.

As more local work becomes delegable, the technical role shifts upstream
toward choosing problems and abstractions, across the system toward defining
interfaces and checks, and downstream toward interpreting uncertainty and
forming the recommendation. This shift does not lift architects above the
engineering details. They retain enough contact with artifacts, tools, and
failure modes to intervene when an abstraction breaks or the evidence no
longer supports the decision.

## Framing the Architecture Problem

Architects do not enter only after a search finishes. Architecture begins
before the candidate set exists and continues after a local result looks
clean. The technical contribution lies in deciding what the system is, which
relationships matter, and which consequences the study must expose. Architects
also create or revise the mechanisms, interfaces, abstractions, and fallback
choices that make specialist results one coherent system. AI may participate
in that work, but the architecture question remains whether those pieces form
a feasible system that meets the product obligation.

Architects also help compose the AI-assisted workflow around that decision.
They determine which method may propose a change, which tool can measure the
relevant property, which check can stop a candidate, and which role resolves
disagreement among returned results. Those choices shape what the study can
observe and which conclusions it can support.

The Lighthouse prompt illustrates the first distinction. A prompt can state an
ambition, but an ambition is not yet an architecture problem. “Design a
low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR
workload” leaves open the representative workloads, supported software path,
product boundary, alternative designs, operating conditions, acceptable
tradeoffs, and decision to be made. Adding more words to the prompt does not
necessarily resolve those choices. Framing turns the ambition into a
challengeable technical question.

The framed problem also determines what the AI-assisted design system must
contain. A study about array utilization may need a cycle-level model and a
mapping search. A decision about freezing the array and its software-facing
interface must also expose compiler and runtime behavior, memory traffic,
implementation feasibility, subsystem power, and the consequences of later
change. The question determines the necessary abstractions and instruments,
not the other way around.

Together, the architecture judgments summarized in
@tbl-architect-technical-judgments turn results from models, tools, and domain
specialists into a coherent product recommendation. Individual judgments may
be distributed by subsystem, property, or design transition, but the architect
or architecture team must still determine whether the domain claims describe
one feasible system.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Problem choice and reframing** | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | The task is not merely to maximize array utilization. It is to decide whether an implementation-facing compute and software interface meets the mobile XR obligation. |
| **Abstraction** | Which details can be simplified for this decision, and which must remain visible? | A cycle-level array model can compare mappings locally, but it cannot hide compiler behavior, memory traffic, physical timing, or the 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| **System boundary** | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Array dimensions and dataflow cannot be separated from the runtime, interconnect, memory, energy, and implementation path they require. |
| **Architecture synthesis** | Do the mechanisms, interfaces, software path, implementation choices, and containment provisions form one feasible system? | The array, compiler and runtime interface, memory path, 3\ W constraint, and fallback behavior must form one implementable subsystem rather than separate local wins. |
| **Missing constraints** | What has the formulation, representation, objective, or tool path left out? | Representative workloads, interface cost, subsystem power, implementation feasibility, reliability and security properties, and containment remain open obligations. |
| **Cross-layer tradeoff** | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Performance, energy, programmability, reversibility, schedule, and review burden must be composed rather than delegated to separate optimizers. |
| **Mechanism and consequence** | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | The failed directional shape-and-mapping explanation cannot support transfer. A wrong freeze could harden a poor software contract and create costly RTL and physical rework. |
| **Commitment under uncertainty** | Are the remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting with the available organizational capacity? | The missing implementation-facing tests block the current freeze. The absent matched comparison independently leaves the AI program test unresolved. |

: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** The
architect chooses the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before
the commitment authority decides whether the design advances.
{#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

A feasible-system claim rests on problem choice, abstraction, and system
boundary. Once those are set, architecture synthesis can expose missing
constraints and cross-layer tradeoffs that separate specialist results
cannot settle.
The mechanism explanation and remaining risk then
determine whether the recommendation can support commitment. In the
Lighthouse, working through these judgments creates and synthesizes
the architecture rather than approving it after the design is complete.

Each judgment depends on the abstractions, components, and constraints that
determine what a local result can mean for the system.

## Choosing Abstractions, Components, and Constraints

An abstraction is a technical choice about which details must remain visible
for a decision and which can be simplified without changing it. The same
candidate may be represented as an instruction mix, a dataflow graph, a
cycle-level model, synthesizable RTL, a floorplan, or a thermal model. None is
the architecture by itself.[^fn-architecture-description-c11] Each exposes some relationships and suppresses
others, so the architect chooses the representation whose omissions are
acceptable for the action under review.

[^fn-architecture-description-c11]: **Architecture description**: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 distinguishes an entity's architecture from an architecture description that expresses it. The standard also specifies requirements for architecture viewpoints and model kinds, but it does not prescribe this chapter's organization, design process, or assignment of authority [@ISOIECIEEE2022ArchitectureDescription].

This choice determines which components can contribute to the decision. The
architect asks what state each predictor, generator, optimizer, conventional
method, or tool may change and which independent observation constrains that
change. Adding components does not necessarily improve the composed system. A
component whose omissions hide a blocking property can make a result less
trustworthy even when its local output improves.

The AlphaChip macro-placement case developed in
@sec-feedback-verification-trust supplies the needed component-versus-system
contrast. The original paper reports the component's macro-placement capability
[@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. That section documents both the dispute over
how far that result holds across tool flows, baselines, and available design
data and the limits of favorable placement proxies. The architecture
consequence is narrower. The architect still sets the block boundaries, macro
set, timing and power
constraints, comparison basis, routability and signoff checks, and determines
whether the placement serves the chip. A capable component can perform
substantive design work without owning the larger technical decision.

Architects also choose how these components interact. They decide which state
crosses an interface, which component may revise it, which independent result
can block progress, and whether two apparent checks share the same assumptions.
The arrangement changes which candidates can be proposed, which properties can
be observed, and which errors can survive.

Some consequential constraints first appear as expert judgment rather than
represented design state. @sec-architecture-20-ontology introduced this as *tacit knowledge*, the
practical knowledge that people use but cannot always state completely
[@Polanyi1966TacitDimension, p. 4]. A compiler specialist may know that a proposed
instruction has no efficient lowering in the supported toolchain. A physical
designer may recognize that a placement heuristic is unsafe for a particular
power-grid geometry and current profile.

A proposed use of AI assistance is to locate, compare, and organize these
judgments for review. Writing them down does not make them authoritative. A
consequential constraint, assumption, or claim needs a check appropriate to its
risk and scope. A qualified automated method, conventional tool, domain
specialist, or independent reviewer may perform that check. The domain
specialist qualifies its meaning and scope, and the architect or architecture
team separately decides whether it belongs in the project record. If accepted,
the architecture team records its source, scope, affected interfaces,
conflicts, expiration, and reopening conditions.

Consider a physical designer's rule against placing two high-current macros on
the same power stripe. The physical-design specialist qualifies the geometry,
current basis, and safe threshold. The architect then decides whether to encode
that knowledge as model state, an environment constraint, a rejection check,
or a scoped specialist judgment, and whether the routing cost still serves the
larger design. A change to the power-grid template invalidates the original
basis and prompts another review rather than leaving the rule in force as
timeless expertise.

Not every expert intuition should become a formal rule. An unrecorded
constraint can be optimized away, while an overgeneralized one can reject good
designs. The distinctive architectural decision is whether the knowledge
belongs in model state, an environment constraint, a rejection check, or
specialist judgment.

The architect must then compose the resulting components and specialist
judgments into one system.

## Integrating Across Layers and Disciplines

A candidate becomes an architecture only when its mechanisms and interfaces
work together across the layers that determine product behavior. For the
Lighthouse, this means connecting the XR workload and algorithms to the
compiler and runtime, instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture,
memory hierarchy and interconnect, RTL, physical design, package, power and
thermal limits, verification, and the user-facing product obligation. A local
improvement may have research or local value even when another layer cannot use
or implement it, but it does not yet establish a usable system result.

Search can find useful candidates and approximate the Pareto frontier
introduced in @tbl-moonshot-decomposition, the feasible objective outcomes not
dominated by another feasible design. Choosing a point on that frontier is a
different act. A wider network link may improve camera-ingest latency while
raising switching activity and routing pressure. A narrower link may save
dynamic power while increasing queueing or software scheduling sensitivity.
Some designs may improve both objectives before the true tradeoff appears. The
architect does not assume conflict in advance. The architect determines which
objectives, constraints, operating conditions, and product consequences make
one feasible point preferable to another.

Once the feasible points are visible, the architect determines which one best
serves the product. The commitment authority turns that recommendation into a
product commitment by authorizing a consequential design transition. The
recommendation includes effects that no one optimizer may
represent, such as software turnover, difficult-to-reverse interfaces,
verification capacity, package constraints, field containment, or a
user-experience threshold. A weighted objective can encode a declared tradeoff,
but it cannot decide whether the weights still represent the product.

The architect or architecture team composes specialist judgments rather than
replacing them. Compiler, verification, physical-design, and product domain
specialists each establish results within their own scope. The architect
determines whether those results address one coherent system decision and
whether an interface between them remains unexamined.

A hypothetical future Lighthouse revision makes this synthesis concrete. Suppose
trace analysis supports the frame-rate target, compiler search finds a legal
tiling, RTL simulation passes, an SRAM model satisfies its local bandwidth
check, and the accelerator block closes timing. When the results are combined,
the tiling raises burst traffic, the wider interface and added buffering push
the subsystem beyond 3\ W, and a tail-latency case has no software fallback.
The architect changes the system by assigning tail handling to the CPU,
narrowing the accelerator interface, revising buffering and scheduling, and
adding a fallback path. Domain specialists then reassess the affected
contracts. No such revision was executed in the retained Lighthouse records.
The sequence illustrates architecture creation because the architect changes
mechanisms, interfaces, and partitioning until the local results describe one
feasible product.

The team must preserve that coherence as work moves among people, models, and
tools. Candidate identity, assumptions, interfaces, checks, and stopping
conditions cannot disappear between components. The architect connects their
outputs from workload behavior through tiling, traffic, buffering, the 3\ W
boundary, and software fallback, then produces one recommendation with explicit
scope, supporting and conflicting results, and known limits. Domain checks
qualify what that recommendation supports. They do not authorize commitment.

## Interpreting Results and Disagreement

A check can support only what its scope, uncertainty, and
independence justify, as @sec-feedback-verification-trust established.
Architecture adds another problem when qualified results disagree.
A result may support a local ranking while its failed mechanism
explanation blocks transfer to a changed workload, software path,
interface, or implementation. The architect must then narrow the
claim, request a discriminating test, or keep the dependent
transition blocked.

The decision cannot be settled by counting votes. The domain specialists
must first determine whether the checks encode the same contract and conditions.
If they do, a blocking failure remains a failure. If they do not, the
architecture problem or interface definition must be corrected and the
affected paths rerun. When domain specialists cannot reconcile the scopes, the
architect or architecture team keeps the transition blocked and escalates the
unresolved system contract rather than choosing the more convenient result.

Consider a coherence verifier that returns a counterexample against a declared
blocking property while the software model treats the same execution as legal.
The proposing system may not weaken the property, remove the failing workload,
or recast the counterexample as a pass. The first technical question is whether
the property and software model encode the same product contract. If they do,
the candidate fails. If they do not, the architecture problem must be corrected
and both paths rerun. The disagreement exposes a system-interface error that
neither local score can settle.

Not every uncertainty blocks all progress. Suppose two feasible candidates
have overlapping estimates for tail latency and subsystem power. The architect
identifies whether workload sampling, model error, or an untested operating
corner could reverse the choice, then requests the least costly higher-fidelity
observation that can discriminate between them, such as matched cycle-level
runs or implementation-facing power analysis. If no available observation can
resolve the overlap within budget, the recommendation remains narrow and the
choice reversible rather than treating the nominal mean as decisive.

Interpretation connects each result to a consequence. A timing pass at one
corner cannot dispose of an open power-delivery failure, and a proof of a
declared property cannot show that the property captured the product behavior.
The architect or architecture team integrates these scoped judgments. That
system-level work does not replace the domain specialists who establish
verification, timing, physical, power-integrity, safety, security, or
reliability signoff.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Architecture judgment does not begin where automation ends"}
Automation may perform substantial local formulation, exploration,
implementation, and analysis, but architecture judgment starts with choosing
the problem, abstraction, and system boundary and continues through cross-layer
synthesis, interpretation of conflicting evidence, and a supported
recommendation. A design review should be able to identify who made those
choices and trace how local results became one feasible system. Without that
basis, a collection of successful tool runs can still support the wrong
architecture. The role may belong to a qualified team rather than one
individual, and automation may contribute to any of its local tasks.
:::

A design commitment requires this integrated account of the architecture
problem, the system, and the meaning of its results.

## Architecture Result, Program Claim, and Commitment

Technical interpretation produces an architecture recommendation, not a
commitment. The recommendation names the preferred design, the credible
alternatives, the conditions and checks that support the comparison, the
conflicting or missing evidence, and the limits that should govern the next
transition. Verification, timing, physical-design, power-integrity, safety,
security, and reliability domain specialists remain responsible for the results and
signoffs within their domains. The architect integrates those results into one
cross-layer recommendation without replacing them.

The two independent tests introduced in @sec-moonshot remain intact.
Architecture evidence establishes what the design supports under the required
workload, software, implementation, physical, and verification checks.
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect separately classifies the program claim as
supported, unsupported, or unresolved by comparing complete approaches. That
status concerns adoption of the approach, not commitment of a particular
architecture, and neither test authorizes a design transition.

For a result in hand, the responsible domain specialist states its validity and
scope. The architect integrates that result with the other qualified evidence
into the cross-layer technical recommendation. The named commitment authority
decides whether this design advances, freezes an interface, enters
implementation, tapes out, or releases. The accountable organization resources
that work, owns the product consequences, and maintains the ability to monitor
and reopen the decision. One person may perform more than one part, but the
qualified result, system recommendation, and authorized decision remain
distinct.

The same study records may feed these judgments, but each answers a different
question. A favorable architecture result does not demonstrate an AI
contribution, and a supported program claim does not authorize a design
transition. Refusing a design also does not by itself make the program claim
unsupported. No result supplies missing evidence for another judgment.

The program claim statuses developed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect leave
different architecture actions open, so none determines the commitment by
itself (@tbl-two-closing-decisions).

| **Program claim status** | **What it means for architecture commitment** |
| --- | --- |
| **Supported** | Repeated matched comparisons across the declared tasks and conditions show that the complete AI-assisted approach clears the relevant architecture-quality or total-cost decision boundary. The architecture may still be refused because the design, evidence, organizational capacity, or residual risk is unacceptable. |
| **Unsupported** | Matched comparisons with sufficient coverage and resolving power show that the claimed advantage does not clear its decision criterion or directly contradict the claim. A sound architecture may still be committed on evidence produced by a conventional or human-directed approach. |
| **Unresolved** | The comparison is missing, incomplete, or underpowered, or its uncertainty prevents determining whether the decision boundary was cleared. No adoption claim is justified. The architecture may proceed only if independent design evidence supports it, or it may remain uncommitted while missing work is completed. |

: **Program claim status and architecture commitment remain independent.**
A favorable result on one cannot substitute for a favorable result on the
other. {#tbl-two-closing-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

The two tests can diverge in either direction. A supported program claim can
accompany a design that should be refused, while an unsupported claim can leave
a sound design backed by conventional work. Evidence for adopting a program or
workflow therefore cannot settle whether a particular architecture should be
committed. The remaining question is what commitment may follow and who owns it.

## Making and Limiting a Design Commitment

An architecture commitment is a technical system choice. It selects a design
and its interfaces for further implementation, product integration, or
release under stated conditions. This chapter treats reversibility as a design
variable. A commitment may remain cheap to revise during early exploration but
become costly once it hardens into an ISA, software interface, floorplan,
package, or mask set. The proposed decision rule is to raise the evidence
burden as reversal becomes more costly and consequential.

The commitment states what design advances, which alternatives were rejected,
which conditions the evidence covered, which uncertainty remains, and what
would invalidate the choice. It does not certify that the design is perfect.
It establishes that the selected system is preferable to the credible
alternatives for the stated product obligation and that the remaining
uncertainty is bounded well enough for the next transition.

Three technical decisions must remain separate. Running work does not establish
what a result supports, and establishing support does not commit the
architecture (@tbl-lighthouse-action-rights).

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execute design work** | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Work stays within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. Execution cannot silently change a requirement or acceptance condition. |
| **Establish what a result supports** | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | The relevant domain specialist owns the result's validity and domain scope; the architect determines how that qualified result applies to the system decision. A waiver or later judgment cannot relabel a failed or inconclusive check. |
| **Commit the architecture** | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition? | The architecture decision composes alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, containment, and residual risk without replacing domain signoff. |

: **Execution, support, and commitment are different technical decisions.**
Separating them prevents a successful tool run or favorable local result from
silently authorizing the architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

A human-automation framework separates information acquisition, analysis,
decision selection, and action implementation, then asks how much of each
function to automate [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation]. It provides a
useful precedent for separating functions before assigning automation. It does
not prescribe this chapter's distinction among executing work, establishing
support, and committing an architecture.

A later judgment cannot rewrite the recorded result of a check. The architecture
team can add results, and changed conditions can invalidate whether the earlier
result still applies to the current candidate. The architect or architecture
team integrates these qualified results but does not replace static-timing,
physical-design, verification, safety, security, or reliability signoff.

The assignment of these decisions differs across organizations. Their
technical meanings should not be collapsed. An AI-assisted system may perform
reversible actions and trigger declared stops, while domain specialists
establish what its results support, the architect integrates those results, and
the commitment authority decides whether the system advances.

### Stating Residual Risk

Commitment does not mean that every uncertainty disappeared. It means the
remaining failure modes are understood well enough to accept, mitigate, or
block. A bounded exception does not change the underlying result, and a
mandatory requirement remains blocking unless the requirement itself changes.
Residual risk is a technical property of the decision, not a label added after
the design advances.

A residual-risk statement is usable only if a reviewer can connect the failure
mode to its consequence, remaining uncertainty, detecting check, and
containment or rollback action. Those five items are the minimum proposed here.
If no check, operating restriction, or containment path can detect or limit the
failure, the design transition remains blocked.

To test what containment would require, consider a hypothetical future
Lighthouse candidate with an optional vector-turbo mode whose subsystem
power and thermal behavior remain insufficiently characterized. This mode is
not part of the retained Lighthouse evidence. Retaining its circuitry for later
study would not justify enabling it. A defensible exception would require a
verified disabled state, an enable path restricted to an authorized lab or
privileged service mode, verified reset, fault, and access-control behavior,
proof that the disabled circuitry does not violate the base design's functional,
timing, power, or security requirements, a named owner, and an expiration tied to
post-silicon characterization. If the disabled state, isolation, or restricted
enable path cannot be validated, the feature is removed or the design does not
advance. The exception does not turn missing evidence into a pass. At
expiration, a new decision must authorize enablement from new evidence, renew a
narrower exception, keep the mode permanently disabled, or remove it.

Repeated exceptions can make a known failure look like the baseline, the
normalization of deviance described by Vaughan
[@Vaughan1996Challenger]. Expiration and reopening keep a temporary decision
from becoming permanent merely because the system stops reporting it. The
transfer concerns repeated acceptance of exceptions. It does not equate chip
review with Challenger's safety stakes or organizational context.

### Design Containment Before Commitment

Containment authority matters only when the design contains a credible
technical lever. Depending on the failure, that lever may be a verified
feature-disable path, safe firmware fallback, derating mode, redundant
resource, isolation boundary, rollback path, or refusal to expose the
capability. Some failures have no safe containment short of repair or
replacement. The absence of a credible lever is itself a reason to refuse a
difficult-to-reverse commitment.

Disable mechanisms are not universal insurance. The disabled state must be
verified, the failure must be isolated from required behavior, and the control
path must remain available under the fault being contained. Errata and later
steppings provide established channels for describing and repairing some
silicon defects, but not every erratum has a workaround and not every later
silicon stepping fixes it.[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]

[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]: **Errata and silicon steppings**: An erratum records a design defect or error that may cause released silicon to deviate from published specifications. A silicon stepping identifies a particular hardware revision. Intel's specification update lists numerous errata for its B2 stepping with the status `No Fix`, illustrating that documenting a defect does not imply that a repair is planned [@Intel2014CoreMIOUpdate].

### The Pending Lighthouse Commitment

Taken together, the missing system-boundary and implementation evidence supports
a technical recommendation to keep the Lighthouse transition open. It does not
show that the design passes or fails, and it does not authorize an architecture
commitment.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
The prospective cache study did not run, and the separate local array result
does not establish the full workload and software interface, the 3\ W subsystem
boundary, or the pinned physical implementation. The architect's present
technical recommendation is therefore to leave the freeze and commitment
undecided pending qualified checks of those requirements. This is a
recommendation to continue the technical work, not a finding that the design
passes or fails and not permission to advance. The two records remain separate
for later review.
:::

A later review must qualify those missing results before the architect can
recommend advancing the design and before the commitment authority can
authorize that transition. A program adoption claim separately requires
repeated matched comparisons of complete approaches.

## Responsibility Continues Through Challenge and Reopening

The accountable organization must be able to challenge and reopen the decision
it makes. Naming an owner does not create this capacity. The candidate,
conditions, alternatives, results, disagreement, and current status must remain
inspectable. The architect or architecture team must have access to the
artifacts and tools that could expose a mistake, as must the domain specialists.

### Maintaining the Capacity to Challenge

Bainbridge's irony of automation is that automation can erode the
practice that once developed human capacity [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].
This is not an argument for keeping routine work manual. It is a reason to
test whether qualified architects and domain specialists can still inspect
tool behavior, failed candidates, and cross-layer diagnoses.

Elish uses *moral crumple zone* for a person who absorbs blame for an automated
system despite lacking meaningful control over its behavior
[@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. Naming a reviewer without access to the decisive
artifacts or authority to stop a transition creates the analogous architecture
risk. *Automation bias* is the tendency to accept incorrect automated advice or
overlook a problem that automation failed to flag. Skitka et al. observed both
errors in a simulated flight task with an imperfect automated aid
[@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias]. That task is not direct evidence about chip
architecture review, and neither lesson establishes a universal review
practice. They motivate an architecture-specific test of whether the proposed
challenge path works.

Challenge capacity has to be demonstrated in technical work. An architect or
domain specialist must be able to reproduce or commission selected decisive
checks, inspect failed candidates, diagnose seeded faults, and reassess the
evidence after a tool or architecture change. At least some exercises should
require an independent initial diagnosis before the automated recommendation
is shown. Each exercise ends with the architect recording how the findings
change the recommendation and the commitment authority deciding whether the
transition advances, narrows, stays open, or reopens. The test connects
technical competence to the decision it is meant to challenge rather than to
generic workforce preservation.

Opaque external dependencies do not make responsibility disappear. A vendor
model, licensed IP block, process design kit, or commercial tool may limit what
the architecture team can inspect. The commitment must identify the exact
version, interface assumptions, available independent checks, and failures that
remain hard to diagnose. If those observations cannot support the required
claim or a safe fallback, commitment is unsound. A vendor certificate
establishes provenance, not an independent technical check.

### Transferring the Technical Basis

The unresolved Lighthouse work makes this continuing responsibility concrete.
An architect or architecture team receiving that work needs its current status,
technical basis, and the conditions that could support a later decision. A
transfer of responsibility must therefore include the technical basis, not just
the report.

Deferred work retains the missing obligations that prevent a decision. A
rejected alternative retains its rejection basis and returns to consideration
only when a relevant condition changes.

The receiving architect or architecture team needs the exact candidate or
release identity, the question and system boundary, the assumptions and
alternatives, the decisive passed, failed, inconclusive, and missing results,
the remaining uncertainty, and any validated containment path. The transfer
must also identify which workload, software, tool, process, interface, or
observed-behavior change would make the earlier decision inapplicable. When
proprietary access limits reproduction, it must state what only a domain
specialist with protected access could inspect.

The architect or successor architecture team initiates technical
reconsideration when one of those conditions changes. It does not personally
repeat every check. It ensures that the affected domain specialists reconsider
the decision and that an earlier result is not reused merely because its report
remains available. The transfer analysis in
@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack addresses what transfers and which dependent
work must be repeated.

### Monitoring and Reopening the Decision

The transferred technical basis determines what monitoring must watch. The
architect identifies which workload mix, software and firmware versions,
operating range, supplier-component versions, tool qualifications, and physical
conditions need continued observation. Product telemetry can expose
changes through tail latency, power and thermal excursions, corrected and
uncorrected errors, reset or retry rates, degraded links, and recurring failure
signatures. Those observations matter only when they are tied to a condition or
failure mode that could change the architecture decision.

A reopening trigger should lead to a named technical action. A changed workload
or software release may require requalifying performance and memory behavior. A
new erratum, supplier revision, or field failure may require a containment
action, a firmware or software change, derating, a feature disable, a new
stepping, or refusal to continue deployment. Specialists establish the affected
results, the architect revises the cross-layer recommendation, the commitment
authority decides the next transition, and the accountable organization owns
the product response. Monitoring is therefore part of maintaining an
architecture decision, not a generic exercise in operating a learned model.

Observed failures can also reopen a commitment. Failing silicon establishes
that a failure occurred under the observed conditions, but not its root cause.
The technical investigation must still distinguish workload, software,
hardware, package, manufacturing, environmental, and operational explanations.

The Pentium FDIV case discussed in @sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive
illustrates the point. Edelman documents five lookup-table entries that
should have returned 2 but instead returned 0
[@Edelman1997PentiumDivision, p. 57]. The defect escaped into released silicon,
but that public account does not
reconstruct every internal handoff. Its role here is narrower. Field evidence
invalidated the confidence behind a released design and demanded renewed
architecture work, containment, and a decision about the affected products.

## Open Questions

The questions across this book mark unresolved
architecture problems rather than a complete research agenda.
They ask what AI-assisted architecture should make
possible and what computer architecture must preserve
as design work changes.

**Maintaining architectural judgment.** As more local work becomes automated,
architecture teams must retain the ability to frame problems, integrate
specialist results, and challenge plausible recommendations.

- **How can an architecture team determine whether it still has the technical
  capacity to challenge an AI-assisted recommendation?** Technical capacity is
  more than access to a checker. Architects must retain enough independent
  understanding to recognize when a plausible cross-layer recommendation
  should be reopened. Architecture practice still lacks a way to recognize the
  loss of that capacity before it causes a consequential failure.

- **Which technical training interventions preserve an architecture team's
  capacity to challenge AI-assisted recommendations?** A credible evaluation
  must measure independent problem framing, detection of unsupported
  cross-layer conclusions, and diagnosis of seeded failures after routine
  design work has been delegated. It remains unclear which interventions
  preserve that capacity and reveal its loss before a consequential decision.

**Assigning authority and responsibility.** Delegated technical work still
requires explicit boundaries among automated systems, domain specialists,
architects, commitment authorities, and the accountable organization.

- **How does dividing technical responsibility change whether an architecture
  team detects and stops an unsupported cross-layer decision?** Different
  assignments determine who can inspect decisive artifacts and who can stop a
  design transition. Experiments with seeded interface contradictions could
  compare detection, access to decisive evidence, and safe stopping without
  assuming that one organization structure is always best.

- **What access and stop authority must accompany responsibility for an
  AI-assisted architecture decision?** A named reviewer cannot be accountable
  without access to decisive evidence or the authority to block an unsupported
  transition. The unresolved issue is what access and authority are sufficient
  at different stakes without turning every technical judgment into centralized
  approval.

**Preserving visibility across system boundaries.** Capable assistance can
expand the work an architecture team delegates only if unfamiliar failures
remain traceable across layers and opaque components.

- **What technical visibility must an architecture team retain to diagnose an
  unfamiliar cross-layer failure?** Useful visibility must connect a symptom in
  one layer to its cause or consequence in another without overwhelming the
  team with every intermediate artifact. The challenge is deciding which
  relationships must remain inspectable as tools and generated components
  change.

- **Which observable interface properties let an architecture team expose
  consequential failures in an opaque supplier or tool component?** Opaque
  components need not reveal their internals, but their interfaces must expose
  enough behavior to detect consequential violations before they propagate
  into the rest of the system. It remains unclear which interface properties
  achieve that balance.

Architecture practice must decide what new capabilities to build and what
judgment, authority, education, interfaces, and diagnostic access it must
preserve.

## Closing the Moonshot

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Delegate technical work, not architectural accountability"}
Technical work may be delegated, but a named, technically qualified,
institutionally empowered authority must be able to stop, commit, or reopen an
architecture decision. The accountable organization owns its consequences and
provides the resources for monitoring and recovery. The commitment authority
need not repeat every delegated tool run or specialist check, but must be able
to inspect the technical basis, keep the recommendation distinct from the
commitment, and accept the consequences of advancing it. A review fails this
principle when responsibility is assigned to someone who cannot inspect
decisive evidence, stop the transition, or obtain the resources needed to
respond after commitment.
:::

The book closes without a Lighthouse verdict. As @sec-running-the-loop
records, the prospective cache study did not run, and the separate executed
array study supports only a local no-change finding for the evaluated array
shapes. It supplies no evidence for the full system, the 3\ W subsystem target,
or the pinned physical implementation. No architecture commitment was recorded.
The missing checks and matched comparison therefore remain future work.

We invite the computer-architecture and machine-learning communities to build
and validate Lighthouse into a maintained community benchmark. No such
benchmark exists yet. A credible benchmark requires a versioned workload,
software stack, and reference design; a declared action space and constraints;
executable tool and evidence tracks; evaluator-owned checks and metrics; matched
conventional and no-added-assistance baselines with total-cost accounting;
retained provenance; contamination controls and task splits; and durable
versioning, maintenance, and governance.

That work preserves the book's two independent tests. The matched comparisons
must establish whether the complete AI-assisted system improves architecture
capability, total cost, or both over a credible alternative within its assessed
envelope. Even if that program claim is supported, the architect must
separately integrate the technical evidence and recommend whether the selected
design and its residual risks justify commitment, and the named commitment
authority must decide whether it advances. If the assessment finds no adoption
advantage, the same architecture may still advance through a conventional
workflow. A component or narrower AI contribution remains unresolved when
controlled replacement or ablation cannot separate it from interactions. The
absence of a verdict cannot become a success claim.

Computer architecture now needs durable cross-layer abstractions that connect
workload and software behavior to microarchitecture and physical
implementation, interfaces that expose assumptions and uncertainty to tools
and reviewers, and evaluations that compare complete approaches rather than
isolated model outputs. It also needs to train architects to design both the
computer system and the AI-assisted design system used to study it.

Architecture 2.0 asks architects to engineer and use an AI-assisted design
system while remaining responsible for the architecture problem, the
cross-layer synthesis, the technical recommendation, and its continued
validity. AI extends the technical work that can be attempted. Architects
decide whether the resulting mechanisms and interfaces form one coherent
system and recommend what should be built. A named commitment authority decides
whether the system advances, and the accountable organization remains
answerable for the product consequences. Architects reopen the technical
recommendation when workloads, software, tools, process conditions, products,
or observed behavior change. That continuing technical work turns capable
automation into architecture.
